current_example.title: Example: Computing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line

q-30045.name: Question 1
q-30045.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/43cff74165732892223841f6780e7aa22c024e3b3c173e60ce15d8d6841a5a08.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $y={x}^{2}-1$ and $y=-\frac{3}{2}x$ for $x\in [-2,\frac{1}{2}]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=5.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-30045.worked_solution:
Let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/7aad98fe0513514aa8827bea4e9ffbac5b70bcb8da7923effd789988c81e286f.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=-\frac{3}{2}x,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y={x}^{2}-1.$

Now, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y={x}^{2}-1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/623b59b7aca8b33c6149ac6b0916d1eeb425adc3f74568868383806cd9b03b12.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}[\,(5)-({x}^{2}-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}{[6-{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y=-\frac{3}{2}x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/c0467a3bf02287589f897586a1358e4abb02759134b6b58622125319dc7331da.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}{[\,(5)-(-\frac{3}{2}x)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}{[5+\frac{3}{2}x]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}{[6-{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}{[5+\frac{3}{2}x]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{1/2}({[6-{x}^{2}]}^{2}-{[5+\frac{3}{2}x]}^{2})\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

q-30045.html:
Question 1
?

The region enclosed by the curves y=x2−1 and y=−32x for x∈[−2,12] is rotated 2π radians about the line y=5. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫−21/2[5+32x]2dx
b
π∫−21/2([5+32x]2−[6−x2]2)dx
c
π∫−21/2([32x]2−[1−x2]2)dx
d
π∫−21/2([6−x2]2+52)dx
e
π∫−21/2([6−x2]2−[5+32x]2)dx
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve y=−32x, and

  • leaves through the outer curve y=x2−1.

Now, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve y=x2−1.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫−21/2[(upper)−(lower)]2dx=π∫−21/2[(5)−(x2−1)]2dx=π∫−21/2[6−x2]2dx.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve y=−32x.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫−21/2[(upper)−(lower)]2dx=π∫−21/2[(5)−(−32x)]2dx=π∫−21/2[5+32x]2dx.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫−21/2[6−x2]2dx−π∫−21/2[5+32x]2dx=π∫−21/2([6−x2]2−[5+32x]2)dx.

q-124601.name: Question 2
q-124601.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/dccfcb991a6c302c522ea73381544d2e6f93b7310f54040151a00832473596b8.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $y=8x$ and $y=-{x}^{4}$ for $x\in [-2,0]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=1.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-124601.worked_solution:
Let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/335b300d66c7a51a37d595f5fb99a281c00ec6a5be62e1be12c2a3104cd54694.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=-{x}^{4},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y=8x.$

Now, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y=8x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/aae56ea01faa2c09f004fe2506c036f4d5e5b2e591e2e653f4794e4a3cecc309.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{0}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{0}[\,(1)-(8x)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{0}{[1-8x]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y=-{x}^{4}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/635d3aabdc16fd90c2e2a06a042f98abe5dc16f1d7747394cd9083858023adee.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{0}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{0}[\,(1)-(-{x}^{4})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{0}{[1+{x}^{4}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{0}{[1-8x]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{-2}^{0}{[1+{x}^{4}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{0}({[1-8x]}^{2}-{[1+{x}^{4}]}^{2})\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

q-124601.html:
Question 2
?

The region enclosed by the curves y=8x and y=−x4 for x∈[−2,0] is rotated 2π radians about the line y=1. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫−20([8x−x4]2−1)dx
b
π∫−20([1−8x]2−[1+x4]2)dx
c
π∫−20(1+8x−x4)2dx
d
π∫−20(x4−8x)2dx
e
π∫−20([8x+1]2−[x4+1]2)dx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve y=−x4, and

  • leaves through the outer curve y=8x.

Now, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve y=8x.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫−20[(upper)−(lower)]2dx=π∫−20[(1)−(8x)]2dx=π∫−20[1−8x]2dx.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve y=−x4.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫−20[(upper)−(lower)]2dx=π∫−20[(1)−(−x4)]2dx=π∫−20[1+x4]2dx.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫−20[1−8x]2dx−π∫−20[1+x4]2dx=π∫−20([1−8x]2−[1+x4]2)dx.

q-30046.name: Question 3
q-30046.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/c2a8da9dd6d088d30b0b023d50ebf2c23e2bcfda89cd390ec16779694ae5eb39.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $y={x}^{3}$ and $y=x$ in the first quadrant is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=2.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-30046.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3} & =x \\ {x}^{3}-x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ x & =-1,0,1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/82783afd970ec3f0e90a8b97a12207b0ed8cbf82323e0512e9fe36b99a6fdc2f.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=x,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y={x}^{3}.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y={x}^{3}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/4a9a72a194226f73da234e03b93e4b255849315808ac948c0958d8dee52b4f73.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(2)-({x}^{3})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[2-{x}^{3}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y=x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/4c53b4b1ad169119cadf490636b12235b3fc225a08d57c11d4f8e26318797f25.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(2)-(x)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[2-x]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[2-{x}^{3}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[2-x]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({[2-{x}^{3}]}^{2}-{[2-x]}^{2})\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

q-30046.html:
Question 3
?

The region enclosed by the curves y=x3 and y=x in the first quadrant is rotated 2π radians about the line y=2. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫01([2−x3]2−[2−x]2)dx
b
π∫01(x−x3)dx
c
π∫−11([2−x]2−[2−x3]2)dx
d
π∫01([2−x3]2−x2)dx
e
π∫−11(x3−x)dx
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

x3=xx3−x=0x(x2−1)=0x=−1,0,1 Hence, our limits of integration are from x=0 to x=1.

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve y=x, and

  • leaves through the outer curve y=x3.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve y=x3.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫01[(upper)−(lower)]2dx=π∫01[(2)−(x3)]2dx=π∫01[2−x3]2dx.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve y=x.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫01[(upper)−(lower)]2dx=π∫01[(2)−(x)]2dx=π∫01[2−x]2dx.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫01[2−x3]2dx−π∫01[2−x]2dx=π∫01([2−x3]2−[2−x]2)dx.

q-30047.name: Question 4
q-30047.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/cf2c500974f9c88751b9dec98cc53b5d3616b736f3ab0504adae5879cac2001a.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $y=2{x}^{2}-2x$ and $y=3-3{x}^{2}$ for $x\in [-\frac{3}{5},1]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=5.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-30047.worked_solution:
Let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/d5593e8c1e1d544acb8824d9428823d3d6cef3971a1cedd4b087a7902b0e2239.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=3-3{x}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y=2{x}^{2}-2x.$

Now, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y=2{x}^{2}-2x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/bddc78f683e28ec6e97fddb32f95dfdaaff27d3aafbdfc61f424857916f81a6c.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{-3/5}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-3/5}^{1}[\,(5)-(2{x}^{2}-2x)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-3/5}^{1}{[5-2{x}^{2}+2x]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y=3-3{x}^{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/cc049c46593baf1d96c04b95680d6b444ab9ceffc64d1f23f310f70e78684c14.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{-3/5}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-3/5}^{1}[\,(5)-(3-3{x}^{2})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-3/5}^{1}{[2+3{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-3/5}^{1}{[5-2{x}^{2}+2x]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{-3/5}^{1}{[2+3{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-3/5}^{1}({[5-2{x}^{2}+2x]}^{2}-{[2+3{x}^{2}]}^{2})\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

q-30047.html:
Question 4
?

The region enclosed by the curves y=2x2−2x and y=3−3x2 for x∈[−35,1] is rotated 2π radians about the line y=5. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫−3/51([5−2x2+2x]2−[2+3x2]2)dx
b
π∫−3/51([7−2x2+2x]2−[5+3x2]2)dx
c
π∫3/51([5−2x2+2x]2+[2+3x2]2)dx
d
π∫3/51(x2+2x−3)2dx
e
π∫−3/51([5+3x2]2−[7−2x2+2x]2)dx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve y=3−3x2, and

  • leaves through the outer curve y=2x2−2x.

Now, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve y=2x2−2x.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫−3/51[(upper)−(lower)]2dx=π∫−3/51[(5)−(2x2−2x)]2dx=π∫−3/51[5−2x2+2x]2dx.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve y=3−3x2.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫−3/51[(upper)−(lower)]2dx=π∫−3/51[(5)−(3−3x2)]2dx=π∫−3/51[2+3x2]2dx.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫−3/51[5−2x2+2x]2dx−π∫−3/51[2+3x2]2dx=π∫−3/51([5−2x2+2x]2−[2+3x2]2)dx.

q-124592.name: Question 5
q-124592.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/ae4ec1bfc4bf15f8ae4d79492389dd6a3fb5e3c504b0d99a43466fc08bd4b63e.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $y={e}^{{x}^{2}}$ and $y={e}^{x+2}$ for $x\in [-1,2]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=-2.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-124592.worked_solution:
Let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/742602117733f7e0f8fa89931ff11cdfa483c3d878a99445ec1408de6aea8f30.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y={e}^{{x}^{2}},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y={e}^{x+2}.$

Now, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y={e}^{x+2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/b6d2a21d75b441ca5c7c76320aad11b4dded17052056f8828e5c93b068b9bad3.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[\,({e}^{x+2})-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[{e}^{x+2}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y={e}^{{x}^{2}}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/1e84714cd64d30cbb4f73c93fc6dfdfeb12f10422f0524d754906709a9a26ff6.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[\,({e}^{{x}^{2}})-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[{e}^{{x}^{2}}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[{e}^{x+2}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}{[{e}^{{x}^{2}}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{2}({[{e}^{x+2}+2]}^{2}-{[{e}^{{x}^{2}}+2]}^{2})\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

The region enclosed by the curves y=ex2 and y=ex+2 for x∈[−1,2] is rotated 2π radians about the line y=−2. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫−12(ex2+2)2dx
b
π∫−12([ex+2+2]2−[ex2+2]2)dx
c
π∫−12(ex+2+2)2dx
d
π∫−12([ex2+2]2−[ex+2+2]2)dx
e
π∫−12((ex+2+2)−(ex2+2))dx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve y=ex2, and

  • leaves through the outer curve y=ex+2.

Now, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve y=ex+2.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫−12[(upper)−(lower)]2dx=π∫−12[(ex+2)−(−2)]2dx=π∫−12[ex+2+2]2dx.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve y=ex2.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫−12[(upper)−(lower)]2dx=π∫−12[(ex2)−(−2)]2dx=π∫−12[ex2+2]2dx.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫−12[ex+2+2]2dx−π∫−12[ex2+2]2dx=π∫−12([ex+2+2]2−[ex2+2]2)dx.

q-361808.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/5a242a5bec4be4cb58b77289ea2ccf49bf22a368c19ec18f10790a417bfbff72.png)

The region shown above enclosed by the curves $y=3-x$ and $y={x}^{2}$ for $x\in [0,1]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=4.$ Find the volume $V$ of the resulting solid. Do not round the answer.

$V=$
{{field-1}}
q-361808.worked_solution:
First, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/255abcfb1a9034df297dc4939d945d8c3b1c4bd717cebde2844aa2a229fd5258.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=3-x,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y={x}^{2}.$

Now, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y={x}^{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/4b480a3bb7312a59edcabb133100bee1ebd5777664ea490b58744171e05e3083.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(4)-({x}^{2})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[4-{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y=3-x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/20de93738463a5b04c0c5c0884d1db7d8867503931122c99a27fc82493b64edb.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(4)-(3-x)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[1+x]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[4-{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[1+x]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({(4-{x}^{2})}^{2}-{(1+x)}^{2})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}-9{x}^{2}-2x+15)\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {(\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}-3{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+15x)|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\pi [(\frac{1}{5}(1)^{5}-3(1)^{3}-(1)^{2}+15(1))-0] \\  & =\pi (\frac{1}{5}-3-1+15) \\  & =\pi (11+\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =\pi (\frac{55}{5}+\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =\frac{56\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.input_html: 56π5​

q-361829.name: Question 7
q-361829.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/778041d84c40044d6f047203a017bd64c0569bcfc9442afca9baa5160b494ae7.png)

The region shown above enclosed by the curves $y=\sqrt{x}+1$ and $y=\frac{x}{2}+1$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=-1.$ Find the volume $V$ of the resulting solid. Do not round the answer.

$V=$
{{field-1}}
q-361829.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x}+1 & =\frac{x}{2}+1 \\ \sqrt{x} & =\frac{x}{2} \\ 2\sqrt{x} & =x \\ x & =0,4\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=4.$

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/7ce02bca7667a9c32971b7840ff2ba4b96ef3a5c9b18aceaeb5b9b713cc7b36f.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=\frac{x}{2}+1,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y=\sqrt{x}+1.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y=\sqrt{x}+1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/6cb557a57a189a426b6cccacd599562332b05aace5bbbfc5d996b0d53fed3359.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}[\,(\sqrt{x}+1)-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}{[\sqrt{x}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y=\frac{x}{2}+1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/26886afd61251cae273c086dba59dcfa912665cdb788b0c3ef866bf61907efa2.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}[\,(\frac{x}{2}+1)-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}{[\frac{x}{2}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}{[\sqrt{x}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}{[\frac{x}{2}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}({(\sqrt{x}+2)}^{2}-{(\frac{x}{2}+2)}^{2})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}(-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-x+4\sqrt{x})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {(-\frac{1}{12}\,{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}+\frac{8}{3}\,{x}^{3/2})|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =\pi ((-\frac{1}{12}\,(4)^{3}-\frac{1}{2}\,(4)^{2}+\frac{8}{3}\,(4)^{3/2})-(0)) \\  & =\pi (8) \\  & =8\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

q-350914.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/8063ba9fbe4c569519eea27e5a5cd69a8f0e708b03d153942fbf22e9345af96a.png)

The region above enclosed by the curves $y={x}^{2}+2$ and $y=20-{x}^{2}$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=20.$ Find the volume $V$ of the resulting solid. Do not round the answer.

$V=$
{{field-1}}
q-350914.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2 & =20-{x}^{2} \\ 2{x}^{2} & =18 \\ {x}^{2} & =9 \\ x & =\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $x=-3$ to $x=3.$

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/f196ef4a3b29a9d62609b0a9290f34d2cb1ef1351baa4883441fd89e9345e4ed.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=20-{x}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y={x}^{2}+2.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y={x}^{2}+2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/c006e66d82e0059b341520bebe983fa75ed144e3050ca8c4493a4b6df3e8f352.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{-3}^{3}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-3}^{3}[\,(20)-({x}^{2}+2)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-3}^{3}{[18-{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y=20-{x}^{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/c91a8e5ed0881ed0c8f34fa2ed6ccb5f95ff75a2f3b48e2d340f8a8856885e3a.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{-3}^{3}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-3}^{3}[\,(20)-(20-{x}^{2})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-3}^{3}{[{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-3}^{3}{[18-{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{-3}^{3}{[{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-3}^{3}((18-{x}^{2})^{2}-({x}^{2})^{2})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-3}^{3}(324-36{x}^{2}+{x}^{4}-{x}^{4})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-3}^{3}(324-36{x}^{2})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {(324x-12{x}^{3})|}_{-3}^{3} \\  & =\pi ((324(3)-12(3)^{3})-(324(-3)-12(-3)^{3})) \\  & =\pi ((972-324)-(-972+324)) \\  & =\pi (648-(-648)) \\  & =1296\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

fields.input_html: 1296π

q-124728.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/efe8084c2e5b9d5eff4f75dffc9acce77aa66ab0dc62c699589573d96f884d49.png)

The region above enclosed by the curves $y={x}^{2}-2$ and $y=-{x}^{2}$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=-2.$ Find the volume of the resulting solid.
q-124728.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2 & =-{x}^{2} \\ 2{x}^{2} & =2 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $x=-1$ to $x=1.$

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/4514019be21deb238c92f557cc041aec9b5e6629bc9d7dcac133a7aa2aed89c7.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y={x}^{2}-2,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y=-{x}^{2}.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y=-{x}^{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/611d10f83c76467c69a1510809738611962dd5d1e1c22a10b0cb3081d2aa52cc.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}[\,(-{x}^{2})-(-2)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}{[2-{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y={x}^{2}-2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/683244c0b5be598da85a8875708f459d4f87319677111f1072c997d911075d68.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}[\,({x}^{2}-2)-(-2)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}{[{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}{[2-{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}{[{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}((2-{x}^{2})^{2}-({x}^{2})^{2})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}(4-4{x}^{2}+{x}^{4}-{x}^{4})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}(4-4{x}^{2})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {(4x-\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3})|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\pi ((4(1)-\frac{4(1)^{3}}{3})-(4(-1)-\frac{4(-1)^{3}}{3})) \\  & =\pi ((4-\frac{4}{3})-(-4+\frac{4}{3})) \\  & =\pi (8-\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =\frac{16\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-124728.html:
Question 9
?

The region above enclosed by the curves y=x2−2 and y=−x2 is rotated 2π radians about the line y=−2. Find the volume of the resulting solid.

a
4π3
b
16π3
c
32π3
d
8π3
e
64π3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

x2−2=−x22x2=2x2=1x=±1 Hence, our limits of integration are from x=−1 to x=1.

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve y=x2−2, and

  • leaves through the outer curve y=−x2.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve y=−x2.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫−11[(upper)−(lower)]2dx=π∫−11[(−x2)−(−2)]2dx=π∫−11[2−x2]2dx.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve y=x2−2.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫−11[(upper)−(lower)]2dx=π∫−11[(x2−2)−(−2)]2dx=π∫−11[x2]2dx.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫−11[2−x2]2dx−π∫−11[x2]2dx=π∫−11((2−x2)2−(x2)2)dx=π∫−11(4−4x2+x4−x4)dx=π∫−11(4−4x2)dx=π(4x−4x33)|−11=π((4(1)−4(1)33)−(4(−1)−4(−1)33))=π((4−43)−(−4+43))=π(8−83)=16π3.

q-3385.name: Question 10
q-3385.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/e8d2665ab162ff21e358a80a6e42659b0385244a08d94f8de3ad5df12b434a9a.png)

The region above enclosed by the curves $y={x}^{2}$ and $y=\sqrt{x}$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=1.$ Find the volume of the resulting solid.
q-3385.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =\sqrt{x} \\ {x}^{2}-\sqrt{x} & =0 \\ \sqrt{x}({x}^{3/2}-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/7aaa03f21130529bdf5572acac29bfe7566724d8acacc99ca5fc0b035de0398b.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=\sqrt{x},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y={x}^{2}.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y={x}^{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/a7bd5b7f8e61be991cb6a54e9b1277bd6df4fd874dbd72ec90802b4f957c31bd.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(1)-({x}^{2})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[1-{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y=\sqrt{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/ee93f00e178fa7fd7b8702538298a15a5c98d94205deeb71401a49d8dd891545.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(1)-(\sqrt{x})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[1-\sqrt{x}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[1-{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[1-\sqrt{x}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}((1-{x}^{2})^{2}-(1-\sqrt{x})^{2})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}-2{x}^{2}-x+2\sqrt{x})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {(\frac{1}{5}\,{x}^{5}-\frac{2}{3}\,{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}+\frac{4}{3}\,{x}^{3/2}\text{ })|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\pi ((\frac{1}{5}\,(1)^{5}-\frac{2}{3}\,(1)^{3}-\frac{1}{2}\,(1)^{2}+\frac{4}{3}\,(1)^{3/2})-(0)) \\  & =\pi (\frac{11}{30}) \\  & =\frac{11\pi }{30}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-3385.html:
Question 10
?

The region above enclosed by the curves y=x2 and y=x is rotated 2π radians about the line y=1. Find the volume of the resulting solid.

a
3π11
b
3π10
c
14π19
d
11π30
e
18π5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

x2=xx2−x=0x(x3/2−1)=0x=0,1 Hence, our limits of integration are from x=0 to x=1.

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve y=x, and

  • leaves through the outer curve y=x2.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve y=x2.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫01[(upper)−(lower)]2dx=π∫01[(1)−(x2)]2dx=π∫01[1−x2]2dx.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve y=x.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫01[(upper)−(lower)]2dx=π∫01[(1)−(x)]2dx=π∫01[1−x]2dx.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫01[1−x2]2dx−π∫01[1−x]2dx=π∫01((1−x2)2−(1−x)2)dx=π∫01(x4−2x2−x+2x)dx=π(15x5−23x3−12x2+43x3/2 )|01=π((15(1)5−23(1)3−12(1)2+43(1)3/2)−(0))=π(1130)=11π30.

q-50324.name: Question 11
q-50324.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/b0e8cbe1a26b5a012f6098b67320070e882fa38783d8eda07dd0b76011a47b21.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x=\frac{1}{y}$ and $x=\frac{5}{2}-y$ is rotated ${360}^{∘}$ about the line $x=-1.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-50324.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{y} & =\frac{5}{2}-y \\ 1 & =\frac{5}{2}y-{y}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-\frac{5}{2}y+1 & =0 \\ 2{y}^{2}-5y+2 & =0 \\ (y-2)(2y-1) & =0 \\ y & =\frac{1}{2},2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $y=\frac{1}{2}$ to $y=2.$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/d5067706f9ff1abbdfd9dfce94711cb854f79c1156ddc0d81c1c35a5ed555f7a.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=\frac{1}{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=\frac{5}{2}-y.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=\frac{5}{2}-y.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/a944979bc352b0e40afea73836b22c1fb1513fabbc727fb60d4c96793ee6fbb5.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{1/2}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1/2}^{2}{[\,(\frac{5}{2}-y)-(-1)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1/2}^{2}{[\frac{7}{2}-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=\frac{1}{y}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/1eb04cf2f3ae0669dd82106b064dd822da618e9ca31bb3b96e4e30c71b7c3193.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{1/2}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1/2}^{2}{[\,(\frac{1}{y})-(-1)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1/2}^{2}{[\frac{1}{y}+1]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1/2}^{2}{[\frac{7}{2}-y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{1/2}^{2}{[\frac{1}{y}+1]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1/2}^{2}({[\frac{7}{2}-y]}^{2}-{[\frac{1}{y}+1]}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}

q-50324.html:
Question 11
?

The region enclosed by the curves x=1y and x=52−y is rotated 360∘ about the line x=−1. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫12([52−y]2−[1y]2)dy
b
π∫12([72−y]2−[1y+1]2)dy
c
π∫1/22([72−y]2−[1y+1]2)dy
d
π∫1/22[72−y]2dy
e
π∫02([72−y]2−[1y+1]2)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation: 1y=52−y1=52y−y2y2−52y+1=02y2−5y+2=0(y−2)(2y−1)=0y=12,2 Hence, our limits of integration are from y=12 to y=2.

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve x=1y, and

  • leaves through the outer curve x=52−y.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve x=52−y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫1/22[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫1/22[(52−y)−(−1)]2dy=π∫1/22[72−y]2dy.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve x=1y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫1/22[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫1/22[(1y)−(−1)]2dy=π∫1/22[1y+1]2dy.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫1/22[72−y]2dy−π∫1/22[1y+1]2dy=π∫1/22([72−y]2−[1y+1]2)dy.

q-125555.name: Question 12
q-125555.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/ac7f02919896aeb40859b1d78608ec7620c26ea77becc806a28d39ef8abacd12.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x=y\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ and $x=2\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ for $y\in [1,2]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=3.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-125555.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/76196a70cdbc65d2f91b4ba500ea83083be5cfe10fe3f3bd09c035e3ea7bcfba.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=2\operatorname{ln}⁡y,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=y\operatorname{ln}⁡y.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=y\operatorname{ln}⁡y.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/e5d8affefbde216fed0bf6acd7d464e921c1cf04e2578050d12c928d6dee5bd0.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(3)-(y\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[3-y\operatorname{ln}⁡y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=2\operatorname{ln}⁡y.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/b4002c7922eac8e7c97d402833eabc3621ed4da2d13799d07206a45cf0afd1f1.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(3)-(2\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[3-y\operatorname{ln}⁡y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{[3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({[3-y\operatorname{ln}⁡y]}^{2}-{[3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡y]}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

q-125555.html:
Question 12
?

The region enclosed by the curves x=yln⁡y and x=2ln⁡y for y∈[1,2] is rotated 2π radians about the line x=3. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫12([3−yln⁡y]2−[3−2ln⁡y]2)dy
b
π∫12([3+yln⁡y]2−[3+2ln⁡y]2)dy
c
π∫12([3−2ln⁡y]2−[3−yln⁡y]2)dy
d
π∫12([3+2ln⁡y]2−[3+yln⁡y]2)dy
e
π∫12([3+yln⁡y]2−[3−2ln⁡y]2)dy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve x=2ln⁡y, and

  • leaves through the outer curve x=yln⁡y.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve x=yln⁡y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫12[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫12[(3)−(yln⁡y)]2dy=π∫12[3−yln⁡y]2dy.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve x=2ln⁡y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫12[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫12[(3)−(2ln⁡y)]2dy=π∫12[3−2ln⁡y]2dy.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫12[3−yln⁡y]2dy−π∫12[3−2ln⁡y]2dy=π∫12([3−yln⁡y]2−[3−2ln⁡y]2)dy.

q-49945.name: Question 13
q-49945.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/1c22369a6f1abc89437de1977135208ef5d0e762a4971df1c9ace14b6af932cd.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x=\frac{5y}{8}$ and $x=\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}$ is rotated ${360}^{∘}$ about the line $x=-2.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-49945.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =\frac{5y}{8} \\ 2{y}^{2} & =5y \\ 2{y}^{2}-5y & =0 \\ y(2y-5) & =0 \\ y & =0,\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=\frac{5}{2}.$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/504e204d73a1f87d72a321e7c0f58eadf01840ff3b8dbc5214f08e50fcbdcf9b.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=\frac{{y}^{2}}{4},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=\frac{5}{8}y.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=\frac{5}{8}y.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/0c43a01a8548112d8dc1f30f9059c560ac7bec1e679a6c76394d83e4bfbea668.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{5/2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{5/2}{[\,(\frac{5}{8}y)-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{5/2}{[\frac{5}{8}y+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/d8478ef13983e6529fa10147f9659171e31a5555cb799ec1fad13d1fe8b25191.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{5/2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{5/2}{[\,(\frac{{y}^{2}}{4})-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{5/2}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{5/2}{[\frac{5}{8}y+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{0}^{5/2}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{5/2}({[\frac{5}{8}y+2]}^{2}-{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+2]}^{2})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

q-49945.html:
Question 13
?

The region enclosed by the curves x=5y8 and x=y24 is rotated 360∘ about the line x=−2. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫05/2[5y8+2]2dy
b
π∫05/2([5y8+2]2−[y24+2]2)dy
c
π∫25([5y8+2]2−[y24+2]2)dy
d
π∫05([5y8]2−[y24]2)dy
e
π∫05([5y8+2]−[y24+2])dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation: y24=5y82y2=5y2y2−5y=0y(2y−5)=0y=0,52 Hence, our limits of integration are from y=0 to y=52.

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve x=y24, and

  • leaves through the outer curve x=58y.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve x=58y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫05/2[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫05/2[(58y)−(−2)]2dy=π∫05/2[58y+2]2dy.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve x=y24.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫05/2[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫05/2[(y24)−(−2)]2dy=π∫05/2[y24+2]2dy.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫05/2[58y+2]2dy−π∫05/2[y24+2]2dy=π∫05/2([58y+2]2−[y24+2]2)dy.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/90980bb04eb7dd9906ec9a99ea3a1b7cfd9c00969bbd9b12c60fe0f80eb88840.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x+2{y}^{2}=1$ and $x=2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{3})$ for $y\in [-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=1.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-125400.worked_solution:
First, since we are rotating about a vertical line, we need to solve the equation of our first curve for $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2{y}^{2} & =1\,⟹\,x=1-2{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/16ca1c96786eb8e7ef12608f70d03b34b679e63d34ef41135b4fd6801bcccc27.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=1-2{y}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{3}).$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{3}).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/276dea7b2d9f50e3fe171cceb64c1c7a12f84cfb18bdbe242102802ad9790f49.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}{[\,(1)-(2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{3}))\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}{[1-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{3})]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}{[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi y}{3})]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=1-2{y}^{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/b6c6fb140bb3eaf4c49cba76af157fb46a568bc2dc24e4763facede62720f844.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}{[\,(1)-(1-2{y}^{2})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}{[2{y}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}({(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi y}{3}))}^{2}-{(2{y}^{2})}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}({cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{2\pi y}{3})-4{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

q-125400.html:
Question 14
?

The region enclosed by the curves x+2y2=1 and x=2sin2⁡(πy3) for y∈[−12,12] is rotated 2π radians about the line x=1. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫−1/21/2(cos2⁡(2πy3)−4y4)dy
b
π∫−1/21/2(sin2⁡(πy3)−4y4)dy
c
π∫−1/21/2(sin2⁡(2πy3)−4y4)dy
d
π∫−1/21/2(cos2⁡(πy3)−(1−2y2)2)dy
e
π∫−1/21/2(cos2⁡(2πy3)−(1−2y2)2)dy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, since we are rotating about a vertical line, we need to solve the equation of our first curve for x:

x+2y2=1⟹x=1−2y2

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve x=1−2y2, and

  • leaves through the outer curve x=2sin2⁡(πy3).

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as a difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve x=2sin2⁡(πy3).

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫−1/21/2[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫−1/21/2[(1)−(2sin2⁡(πy3))]2dy=π∫−1/21/2[1−2sin2⁡(πy3)]2dy=π∫−1/21/2[cos⁡(2πy3)]2dy.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve x=1−2y2.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫−1/21/2[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫−1/21/2[(1)−(1−2y2)]2dy=π∫−1/21/2[2y2]2dy.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫−1/21/2((cos⁡(2πy3))2−(2y2)2)dy=π∫−1/21/2(cos2⁡(2πy3)−4y4)dy.

q-125546.name: Question 15
q-125546.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/559548dc5f2570d1341760ab87a2619646ed6985fd6437cb29442dc58bc6fee4.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x={y}^{2}+2y-1$ and $x=-1-{y}^{2}$ is rotated ${360}^{∘}$ about the line $x=-2.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-125546.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2y-1 & =-1-{y}^{2} \\ 2{y}^{2}+2y & =0 \\ 2y(y+1) & =0 \\ y & =-1,0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $y=-1$ to $y=0.$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/8f1bccafe64a6926bdb214410453cecafa7059f74a539b155a4a4e6cccd67d1a.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x={y}^{2}+2y-1,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=-1-{y}^{2}.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=-1-{y}^{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/7d1d1ed82fadf105997e00d39b99992cdeba1d41be13cf599db63b34902e149a.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}[\,(-1-{y}^{2})-(-2)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}{[1-{y}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x={y}^{2}+2y-1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/040e0a87b4bb5c7121a27fd2cc94c520f76919afbb86a49cfed2ed0cf57c1561.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}{[\,({y}^{2}+2y-1)-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}{[{y}^{2}+2y-1]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}{[{y}^{2}+2y+1]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}{[1-{y}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}y-\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}{[{y}^{2}+2y+1]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}({[1-{y}^{2}]}^{2}-{[(y+1)^{2}]}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}({(1-{y}^{2})}^{2}-(y+1)^{4})\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

q-125546.html:
Question 15
?

The region enclosed by the curves x=y2+2y−1 and x=−1−y2 is rotated 360∘ about the line x=−2. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫−10((y2+1)2−(y+1)4)dy
b
π∫−10((1−y2)2−(y+1)4)dy
c
π∫−20((1−y2)2−(y2+2y−3)2)dy
d
π∫−10((1−y2)2−(y2+1)2)dy
e
π∫−20((y2+1)2−(y2+2y)2)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation: y2+2y−1=−1−y22y2+2y=02y(y+1)=0y=−1,0 Hence, our limits of integration are from y=−1 to y=0.

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve x=y2+2y−1, and

  • leaves through the outer curve x=−1−y2.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve x=−1−y2.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫−10[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫−10[(−1−y2)−(−2)]2dy=π∫−10[1−y2]2dy.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve x=y2+2y−1.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫−10[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫−10[(y2+2y−1)−(−2)]2dy=π∫−10[y2+2y−1]2dy=π∫−10[y2+2y+1]2dy.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫−10[1−y2]2dy−π∫−10[y2+2y+1]2dy=π∫−10([1−y2]2−[(y+1)2]2)dy=π∫−10((1−y2)2−(y+1)4)dy.

q-86194.name: Question 16
q-86194.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/6ba207cd34725ec2e3995eb0f90e63bedc8573300335b2d31163457ef8ee9bad.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x={y}^{2}+1$ and $x=2{y}^{2}$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=-2.$ Find the volume of the resulting solid.
q-86194.worked_solution:
First, to determine the limits of integration, we find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2} & ={y}^{2}+1 \\ {y}^{2} & =1 \\ y & =-1,1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $y=-1$ to $y=1.$

Next, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/41f8dff0676c5cf8952f46b174ff4f98deeb97eec272e417f145b4782770c156.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=2{y}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x={y}^{2}+1.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x={y}^{2}+1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/b4d3d75dfab4aa6382bf47f06a57036ec612a05c90d0764cd48fdc1f150f2453.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}{[\,({y}^{2}+1)-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}{[{y}^{2}+3]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=2{y}^{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/6f79c95e2b2d3aaf71e6dfac5ca93fa20261f5f40e1660cefc4ac23af3e56cf8.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}{[\,(2{y}^{2})-(-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}{[2{y}^{2}+2]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}({[{y}^{2}+3]}^{2}-{[2{y}^{2}+2]}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}(-3{y}^{4}-2{y}^{2}+5)\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {(-\frac{3{y}^{5}}{5}-\frac{2{y}^{3}}{3}+5y)|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\pi [(-\frac{3\cdot {1}^{5}}{5}-\frac{2\cdot {1}^{3}}{3}+5\cdot 1)-(-\frac{3\cdot (-1)^{5}}{5}-\frac{2\cdot (-1)^{3}}{3}+5\cdot (-1))] \\  & =\frac{112\pi }{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-86194.html:
Question 16
?

The region enclosed by the curves x=y2+1 and x=2y2 is rotated 2π radians about the line x=−2. Find the volume of the resulting solid.

a
12π15
b
112π15
c
12π5
d
11π5
e
11π15
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, to determine the limits of integration, we find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

2y2=y2+1y2=1y=−1,1

Hence, our limits of integration are from y=−1 to y=1.

Next, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve x=2y2, and

  • leaves through the outer curve x=y2+1.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve x=y2+1.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫−11[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫−11[(y2+1)−(−2)]2dy=π∫−11[y2+3]2dy.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve x=2y2.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫−11[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫−11[(2y2)−(−2)]2dy=π∫−11[2y2+2]2dy.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫−11([y2+3]2−[2y2+2]2)dy=π∫−11(−3y4−2y2+5)dy=π(−3y55−2y33+5y)|−11=π[(−3⋅155−2⋅133+5⋅1)−(−3⋅(−1)55−2⋅(−1)33+5⋅(−1))]=112π15.

q-30118.name: Question 17
q-30118.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/c62793a0dc7ff37a4d6b7cf157239f21e6b0cdef8c3d428916f074584462598b.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $y={x}^{2}$ and $y=3x$ for $y\in [0,9]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=5.$ Find the volume of the resulting solid.
q-30118.worked_solution:
First, since we are rotating about a vertical line, we need to solve the equations of our curves for $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={x}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{y} \\ y & =3x\,⟹\,x=\frac{1}{3}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/bd75a7448cfda8237a403f4ea67a99c38e41788839f5c88b89487106e49547d3.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=\sqrt{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=\frac{1}{3}y.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=\frac{1}{3}y.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/0ec13c4447954916af6e3b72abffefb69a46a12671b7b8388a873835654ec921.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{9}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{9}{[\,(5)-(\frac{1}{3}y)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{9}{[5-\frac{1}{3}y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=\sqrt{y}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/7404d889d1388540821bbd282f82322e3249534b8d4518a6236e9f4bf3164d2c.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{9}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{9}[\,(5)-(\sqrt{y})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{9}[5-\sqrt{y}]^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{9}({(5-\frac{1}{3}y)}^{2}-{(5-\sqrt{y})}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{9}(\frac{1}{9}{y}^{2}-\frac{13}{3}y+10\sqrt{y})\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {(\frac{20{y}^{3/2}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{27}-\frac{13{y}^{2}}{6})|}_{0}^{9} \\  & =\pi [(\frac{20\cdot {9}^{3/2}}{3}+\frac{{9}^{3}}{27}-\frac{13\cdot {9}^{2}}{6})-0] \\  & =\frac{63\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

y=x2⟹x=yy=3x⟹x=13y

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve x=y, and

  • leaves through the outer curve x=13y.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve x=13y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫09[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫09[(5)−(13y)]2dy=π∫09[5−13y]2dy.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫09[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫09[(5)−(y)]2dy=π∫09[5−y]2dy.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫09((5−13y)2−(5−y)2)dy=π∫09(19y2−133y+10y)dy=π(20y3/23+y327−13y26)|09=π[(20⋅93/23+9327−13⋅926)−0]=63π2.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/b0aa7d362596dcea976fead0467b9eb76c04b85c02c55dbd12e9a95652eda276.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $y=x$ and $y=\sqrt{x}$ for $y\in [0,1]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=3.$ Find the volume of the resulting solid.
q-85687.worked_solution:
First, since we are rotating about a vertical line, we need to solve the equations of our curves for $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}y=x & \,⟹\,x=y \\ y=\sqrt{x} & \,⟹\,x={y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/f15165acc18f4cf828671e3f9085274b26598a643be9eeb97be617272d7008d7.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=y,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x={y}^{2}.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x={y}^{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/54820b3b386c9a435de04e0b3f07d4e2221a3e026ba5ba93ca25fa6640aa0ab1.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[\,(3)-({y}^{2})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[3-{y}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=y.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/3e1a6067500f81cabeac8dc43c4c585da608ea655667dc5e00f29a6fad0dda60.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(3)-(y)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[3-y]^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({(3-{y}^{2})}^{2}-{(3-y)}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{4}-7{y}^{2}+6y)\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {(\frac{{y}^{5}}{5}-\frac{7{y}^{3}}{3}+3{y}^{2})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\pi [(\frac{{1}^{5}}{5}-\frac{7\cdot {1}^{3}}{3}+3\cdot {1}^{2})-0] \\  & =\frac{13\pi }{15}.\end{aligned}

q-85687.html:
Question 18
?

The region enclosed by the curves y=x and y=x for y∈[0,1] is rotated 2π radians about the line x=3. Find the volume of the resulting solid.

a
π5
b
13π15
c
π15
d
11π15
e
3π5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, since we are rotating about a vertical line, we need to solve the equations of our curves for x:

y=x⟹x=yy=x⟹x=y2

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve x=y, and

  • leaves through the outer curve x=y2.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve x=y2.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫01[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫01[(3)−(y2)]2dy=π∫01[3−y2]2dy.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve x=y.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫01[(right)−(left)]2dy=π∫01[(3)−(y)]2dy=π∫01[3−y]2dy.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫01((3−y2)2−(3−y)2)dy=π∫01(y4−7y2+6y)dy=π(y55−7y33+3y2)|01=π[(155−7⋅133+3⋅12)−0]=13π15.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/64b0f84b62adc0db3385a75d8fdc6e6707eb6778084b9e21de863ca6954c4c1d.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $x+{y}^{2}=25$ and $x+5y=25$ for $y\in [0,5]$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=25.$ Find the volume $V$ of the resulting solid. Do not round the answer.

$V=$
{{field-1}}
q-351346.worked_solution:
First, since we are rotating about a vertical line, we need to solve the equations of our curves for $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+{y}^{2} & =25\,⟹\,x=25-{y}^{2} \\ x+5y & =25\,⟹\,x=25-5y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's draw a horizontal arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/f5b7cafc0ad6ab7624c1274451f16ba2c3c9a111ac9dad3abd90f082cc42d9b9.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $x=25-{y}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $x=25-5y.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $x=25-5y.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/166dbb3f75000dfc155abfc3452ff6874dab1542409edc7e4867c5a5ee73c0b0.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{5}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{5}{[\,(25)-(25-5y)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{5}{[5y]}^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $x=25-{y}^{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/9322b6f4bc9a0e913670f8dcbc9657206c3ae6a30de2f26308054d75b67d0861.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{5}[\,(\text{right})-(\text{left})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{5}[\,(25)-(25-{y}^{2})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{5}[{y}^{2}]^{2}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{5}({(5y)}^{2}-{({y}^{2})}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{5}(25{y}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {(\frac{25{y}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{5}}{5})|}_{0}^{5} \\  & =\pi [(\frac{25(5)^{3}}{3}-\frac{(5)^{5}}{5})-0] \\  & =\pi (\frac{3125}{3}-625) \\  & =\frac{1250\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
